skyline.text: Where is the coercion? Amit Varma finds it in the state
Why Ajay Shah would hand out IIT seats at random
China shut its test-prep industry in one swoop. Should India?

brief.head: The whipped creme
brief.text: Ajay Shah questioned the narrowness of the so-called creme of the country. “When I was in IIT,” he recalled, “we used to be called the whipped creme.” {070-J04}

brief.head: Fastest gun
brief.text: Coaching classes reduce the exam to 1,700 question types, Ajay Shah said. A drilled topper is quick “not because you’re so smart, but because you’ve seen them before”. {070-J05}

brief.head: Mind the bureaucrats
brief.text: Amit Varma: “Never trust a joint secretary.” Ajay Shah: “Education is too important to be left to education bureaucrats.” Both were objecting to one national policy for every college. {070-J08}

brief.head: The English advantage
brief.text: Interviews beat marks alone, Amit Varma agreed, but they massively favour the privileged who grew up speaking English at home. He would weigh several factors instead. {#english}

brief.head: Robots, not marks
brief.text: Kavi Arya’s E-Yantra challenges students to build a robot that does X. With no certificate, exam or marks, Ajay Shah said, the only reward is the pleasure of doing it. {070-R14}

thought.text: You need a liberal democracy with free markets for good solutions to come about.
thought.who: Amit Varma, turning down Ajay Shah’s offer to make him dictator of education

lead.kicker: Amit Varma and Ajay Shah on India’s entrance exams
lead.head: Many are coached, few are chosen
body: Amit Varma says he chose his co-host by entrance exam. It had one multiple-choice question, and Ajay Shah, offered all the money and fame in the world, a private jet or Instagram stardom, picked “freedom for everyone”. {070-J01}
India’s real entrance exams, the hosts agreed, are no joke. “In India, this is a bloody mess,” Shah said. “Everything about it is broken.”
There are very few seats and insane levels of competition, he said. A whole industry teaches to the test, the stress is high, and students try the exams for years.

Varma located the heart of it in a mismatch of supply and demand: very few seats, and many, many students who want them. Coaching institutes are everywhere. “Every year you hear about suicides in Kota,” he said. “It has become an industry.”
## The myth of merit
Shah went after the claim that gives the system its moral legitimacy: that more marks in the JEE mean more intelligence and more knowledge. “I no longer believe that,” he said.

A high-stakes exam has only so many question types, he argued, so coaching turns it into pattern recognition. “It is unintelligent in exactly the way that computer systems are unintelligent,” he said. {070-C02}
The one trait it rewards is conscientiousness: children who obey, drill from morning to night and shut out every other kind of knowledge. India, Shah said, is misallocating its scarce seats.
## Within the system

Varma posed what he calls Varma’s Question: where is the coercion? {070-C01} There is none in children going to coaching classes, he said. They are the market’s answer to a broken system, and banning them would be absurd.

Shah offered three fixes that work within the paradigm. Run computerised tests, drawn at random from a question bank, about 250 days a year, and count each candidate’s best of two or three attempts. Make the tests adapt to the candidate. Hand the work to private firms.
Going deeper, Shah argued that colleges should be free to choose their own students and to look at the whole person, as the IIMs do with group discussions and interviews.
## A friendly fight

Then came what Varma billed as the masala. Shah and Nitin Pai propose an exam at about 17 to find the top one lakh students, then a lottery among them for the 20,000 IIT seats. Parents, Shah said, need not bother with Kota. {070-C07}
Varma was not having it. “I have great fondness for both you and Nitin and great respect,” he said. “But in this matter, you are both wrong.”
The plan, he said, was “an excellent technocratic design of a bad solution”. It missed the point: there are not enough seats.

“Today everyone in India who wants to get a shampoo can buy a shampoo,” Varma said. Good education, by contrast, is kept scarce by the state, through licences, a ban on profit, land rules and PhD requirements for faculty. Shah agreed, adding that only politicians start universities in India.
For parents and students, Shah’s advice was to look past the brand names of IIT and MIT, and at the person in the mirror. Checking out of the rat race, he said, “should be perfectly okay”. {070-C12}
His ideal is a child who grows up excited and happy, perhaps taking an interest in organic chemistry or the electric guitar, and who knows about the world.

second.label: Testing, statistically
second.head: Not an objective truth
second.deck: Ajay Shah wants India’s exams built by statisticians, one question at a time
body: “An exam is not an objective truth,” Ajay Shah said. “An exam is a statistical estimator of the knowledge of the test taker.” So look for its bias and its error variance, he argued, and work to reduce both. {070-C04}

His tool is item response theory, used in the GRE and the SAT: easy questions first, harder ones once you ace them. In India, Shah said, where some 1 per cent get through, it is the top tail that must be told apart. {#onepercent}
Each reused question goes under the microscope: if strong candidates do not get it right more often than weak ones, the question is faulty. As for UPSC papers, Shah said, “they are nonsense”. {#upsc}

quote.text: We should not be so reverential about these exams.

second.caption: the exam as a statistical estimator

third.head: Lights, camera, lecture
body: Amit Varma will not call it a solution, because solutions go to root causes. It is a jugaadu hack. “Put one frickin’ video camera, record it, put it online,” he urged every college. {#camera}
Teachers would feel more accountable, he said. Those who did not make it through would still get the knowledge, if not the network or the credentials.
His example is Robert Sapolsky’s biology lectures, free on YouTube. Varma had never been interested in biology, he said, but Sapolsky “just opens your mind up in different ways”. {070-R10}

Ajay Shah said IIT Bombay already does this, taking its engineering teaching on video to hundreds of thousands of students. “If there is knowledge inside IIT Bombay, it is available,” he said. “The rest is just credentialism and is less important.” {070-C11}
third.caption: knowledge without the credential

p2.title: The fix is in
p2.deck: From the myth of merit to the root cause, Ajay Shah’s reforms and Amit Varma’s objections, chapter by chapter

sections.label: The diagnosis
sections.head: Merit by rote
sections.caption: the meritocracy myth
body: The system’s moral legitimacy, Ajay Shah said, rests on one claim: that the student with more marks in the IIT JEE is more intelligent, more knowledgeable and better suited to an engineering education. “I no longer believe all these things,” he said.

His reason is the high-stakes exam itself. A school-leaving test can ask only so much of a twelfth-standard child, so coaching classes analyse past papers and boil it down to 1,700 question types. Work two days on each, and in 3,400 days you are ready. {#types}
What results is table lookup: see this type of question, jump to that solution. It is unintelligent, Shah said, in exactly the way that computers are. {070-C02}
## One trait among many

Human capability, he argued, is curiosity, tenacity, innovation, creativity and flexible general intelligence. The exam rewards only conscientiousness: children who obey, work from morning to night and “just memorise the reactions of benzene”. {#benzene}
Each family is behaving sensibly, Shah granted: in a society of credentialism, chasing an IIT degree is incentive compatible. But the country misallocates its seats, and its children’s hours.

~ Amit Varma agreed. The exam, he said, has become a game within a game, about admissions rather than knowledge: “We have two seats and eighty-five people who want to be in those two seats.” {#twoseats}

quote.text: We are not getting the best kids into the IITs. We are getting the kids who have the ability to be regimented.

sections.label: Varma’s question
sections.head: Don’t ban the paracetamol
sections.caption: banning the coaching classes
body: Ajay Shah, needling, offered an easy way out. “Our dear friend Xi Jinping” had shut down China’s entire test-prep industry in one fell swoop. Free markets are all very well, he teased, “but in this one case, you’ve really got to give it because of the plight of the children.” {070-J02}

Amit Varma called it an absurd solution, and answered with Varma’s Question: where is the coercion? Not in the coaching classes, he said. Children go because the system demands it of them, and the market serves them. {070-C01}
## Fever and pills

Suppose you run a fever of 103 every day and end up taking three paracetamols a day. “Is the solution to this banning paracetamols? Of course not,” Varma said. You find what is causing the fever. {070-C03}

Banning a victimless activity, he argued, merely drives it underground. Prohibit liquor and it comes from the black market, dearer and worse, and people die of hooch poisoning. A ban on prostitution brings trafficking and coercion.
~ The real coercion, Varma promised, lay somewhere else, and he would get to it by the end of the episode.

quote.text: Whenever there is a problem in society or public policy, the first question I want to ask is where is the coercion?

sections.label: Three quick fixes
sections.head: Every day is exam day
sections.caption: the three-part solution
body: Staying inside the paradigm, Ajay Shah offered three fixes. The first ends the single exam on a single day, which today sends two and a half million children to test centres across the country. {#onesingle}

States learn only by doing things repeatedly, he said. So run a computerised test, generated at runtime from a large question bank, for 250 days a year: 10,000 candidates a day. Let each take it two or three times and keep the best score, in case of a heat wave, bad air or a bad day. {070-C05}
None of it is new. Shah had helped NSE build just such an exam for derivatives traders, and ETS runs the SAT and GRE this way.
## Better maths, private hands

The second fix is item response theory, which adjusts the questions to the candidate. The third is to let private firms run the tests, since governments, Shah said, are not good at running airlines, payment systems or banks. {#private}
~ Amit Varma loved all of it, and was reminded of his chess puzzles. His one caveat: these were “fantastic technocratic solutions” that did not reach the root cause.

quote.text: It’s much better to do things repeatedly and mistakes will happen and there will be feedback loops and you’ll get things better.

sections.label: Free the colleges
sections.head: Berkeley is not Los Angeles
sections.caption: letting colleges pick their students
body: The most important piece, Ajay Shah said, is to end centralisation. A university gets better only when it has autonomy, a sense of mission and the power to make its own decisions, year after year.
It is as wrong to force all the IITs to be alike, he argued, as to run every public sector bank as one. {070-C06}
Admission to the University of California, Berkeley is fully distinct from admission to its Los Angeles sibling, Shah pointed out, though both sit in the state’s UC system. {#berkeley}

A motivated university can calibrate CBSE marks against ICSE ones, he said, and the Los Angeles campus compares applicants from every school system in the world. “It’s not that hard to figure out who is a good candidate.”
## See the whole person
Shah wants India out of the test mentality. The IIMs use a group discussion and an interview, and economics PhD admissions now include a video interview. {#iims}
Amit Varma agreed, with a caveat: interviews favour the privileged who grew up speaking English at home, so they work best as one factor among several.
~ Colleges, Varma said, should be able to compete on how well they select bright people. One might want a liberal-arts bent, Shah added, another a business-school one.

quote.text: It is exactly as wrong to try to force all the IITs to be alike or all universities in India to be alike.

sections.label: The lottery
sections.head: Luck of the draw
sections.caption: the Pai-Shah lottery
body: Ajay Shah and Nitin Pai propose two stages. First, an all-India conceptual exam at about 17, hard to game with test prep, in which the goal is the top one lakh rather than the top thousand. {#toplakh}

Shah pegged the bar at roughly 650 on the OECD’s PISA test, which he called more conceptual and not something you can train for. Then the 20,000 IIT seats are drawn by lottery from the one lakh. {#stage2}

He saw three gains: more varied IIT batches, professors forced to raise their teaching, and 80,000 strong students lifting classrooms across India. A normal school education, plus football and curiosity, would be enough. {070-C07}
## You are both wrong

Amit Varma, who had promised a fight, said the plan was being compared in an idealised form with the real system. It does not reward desire or hard work, he said: for some, the top one lakh “would just be a breeze”.
Then there is allocation. A child desperate to study mechanical engineering could lose out to one who wants to write poems, “and both of us will be miserable for the rest of our lives”. {#poems}
~ Similar lotteries for medicine in the Netherlands and New Zealand, Varma said, have drawn criticism.

quote.text: The scheme that you laid out with the numbers that you laid out are an excellent technocratic design of a bad solution

sections.label: The root cause
sections.head: Shampoo galore, seats rationed
sections.caption: where the coercion lies
body: “Today everyone in India who wants to get a shampoo can buy a shampoo,” Amit Varma said. Education, by contrast, is kept scarce, and India has normalised it. {070-C09}

Offered the post of dictator by Ajay Shah, Varma balked: a dictator, he said, makes a good solution impossible. {070-J07} Then he answered his own question: the coercion comes from the state, standing in the way of private entrepreneurs who would set up colleges.

To start one, you need licences and permissions that can take years. Land and infrastructure mandates follow, and rules that faculty must hold PhDs. Hiring Varma, who has none, to teach podcasting or writing should be a “no-brainer”, he said. {#podcasting}
## A dirty word

Then there is the mandate that higher education cannot be run for profit. Founders resort to jugaad with trusts, at great friction and cost. “To me, profit is the best kind of philanthropy,” Varma said, because in a free market you profit only by making someone better off. {070-C10}

Shah agreed. Because starting a university is so hard, only politicians do it, and they are not the people best equipped to. {#politicians} He is optimistic about Ashoka, FLAME and Nayanta, but asked why so few are allowed.
~ The same holds for medicine, Shah said: India simply does not have enough medical colleges.

quote.text: We have normalised the fact that good quality education is a scarce resource.

side.boxText: Ajay Shah’s lottery plan is set out in *Doing better than a competitive exam*, written with Nitin Pai. The two drew on ideas from all over the world, Shah said, and adapted them to Indian conditions. {#pai}

contQuote.text: These are human beings and we need to nurture and grow their intellectual and emotional capacity. That’s what growing up is about. That’s what education is about.

p3.title: Tales from the exam hall
p3.deck: A swimming test, a chess rating, a teenage hacker and a traders’ exam

stories.start: Our mutual friend Deeper Quias uh did uh this great episode
stories.end: you have the same problems that we have with the current system
stories.caption: the swimming test
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on a thought experiment from Deepak VS
stories.head: Sink or swim into the IITs
body: Deepak VS, a friend of both hosts and a guest on Amit Varma’s podcast *The Seen and the Unseen*, is always throwing out thought experiments. On that show he once threw a hypothetical at Varma: scrap the IIT entrance exam, and replace it with a swimming test. {070-S04}
Varma brought it up in the middle of his fight with Ajay Shah over Shah’s lottery for IIT seats. It was related, he said, though not one of his criticisms.
There was a logic to the swimming test. In Varma’s words, you would at least be selecting for desire. India has coastline across the country, and could set up swimming pools.
Such thought experiments, he said, are a great way to denormalise things and think about them.

Then came the twist. “Now obviously year two, year three, everything goes to hell,” Varma said. Coaching classes start, and the whole business gets institutionalised, with “IIT coaches and Speedos on billboards”.
Before long, he said, “you have the same problems that we have with the current system”. The disease, as he would argue later in the episode, is the scarcity of seats, not the particular test.

~ Varma had made a similar joke at the very start. If Shah said anything against freedom, he warned, he might have to fire him and hold another entrance exam for a co-host, “and now everybody will game it because they know the answer”. {#game}
stories.why: Any single high-stakes filter guarding a scarce prize gets gamed by an industry built around it. Swap the exam for a swim and the coaching follows, Speedos and all. Varma’s answer is more seats. {070-C09}
stories.postscript: Varma recommended his conversation with Deepak VS, *Deepak VS and the Man Behind His Face*, for more such thought experiments.

stories.start: it reminds me of a delightful session we had, Ajaisha, where you uh sat
stories.end: as a recreational player who never tries to improve
stories.caption: the chess.com puzzle rating
stories.kicker: Amit Varma on chess puzzles and adaptive testing
stories.head: Grandmaster, on paper
body: Ajay Shah’s idea of a test that adapts to the candidate reminded Amit Varma of a delightful session at his laptop, solving chess puzzles on chess.com while Shah sat beside him.
The site works the way Shah wants exams to work. As your rating rises, the puzzles get tougher; slip, and they get easier. That day, Varma reached 2900. {070-S01}

“With great awe in your eyes,” Varma reminded Shah, “you asked that, I mean, does this mean that you’re equal to a 2900 in the real world.” It did not. His actual rating, he said, is around 1900 to 2000. {#elo}
~ Shah held that 2900 was still super cool. Varma was unmoved: there is massive inflation in puzzle ratings, “so it’s not that cool”.
stories.why: A score means something only relative to what it measures. A puzzle rating that rises and falls with each answer is a familiar version of the adaptive testing Shah wants for India’s entrance exams. {070-C04}

stories.start: There used to be an exam called the NTS, the National Talent Search.
stories.end: ten standard child, not just like grind them into an exam
stories.caption: the National Talent Search interview
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on an exam that asked about his hobbies
stories.head: The boy who hacked circuits
body: Long ago, Ajay Shah recalled, India had an exam called the NTS, the National Talent Search. As he remembered it, a third of the weight went to an IQ test, a third to a bunch of subjects and a third to an interview.
So a panel sat Shah down, a tenth-standard child, and asked what he did in his spare time. “I hack electronic circuitry,” he said. {070-S02}
“So they said, Tell us about your electronic circuitry.” That, Shah said, is the right way to talk to a child of that age, “not just like grind them into an exam”.
~ If the IIMs can weigh interviews and group discussions, he asked, why can’t the IIT entrance? {#iims}
stories.why: India once ran a high-stakes selection that treated a teenager as a whole person, not a machine for producing marks. Shah’s point is that admission to the IITs could also look beyond a single test.

stories.start: many years ago, I I helped NSE build a certification exam
stories.end: take an appointment and you take the test as and when you please
stories.caption: the NSE certification exam
stories.kicker: Ajay Shah on a reform India has already tried
stories.head: Book a slot, sit the test
body: Many years ago, Ajay Shah helped NSE build a certification exam for traders who wanted to do derivative trading.

Test-taking centres were set up all over the country. “We developed a question bank once,” he said, “and then a random subset of those questions is shown to each person.” Candidates booked an appointment and took the test whenever they pleased. {070-S03}
Shah told the story to show that his first reform for India’s entrance exams, a computerised test that runs all year, is nothing new, and has been run in India before.
~ The SAT and the GRE, he noted, already run this way, through a private firm called ETS. “I’m not saying anything novel,” he said. {#ets}
stories.why: The obstacle to better exams, the story suggests, is not technical know-how. It is the habit of holding one giant state-run exam on one single day, for two and a half million children. {#onesingle}

quiz.q: In the cold open, which option did Ajay Shah pick in Amit Varma’s one-question entrance exam?
quiz.a: None of these, but freedom for everyone, over money, fame, a jet or Instagram.

quiz.q: What is Varma’s Question, which Amit Varma asks first of any problem in society or policy?
quiz.a: Where is the coercion? The answer usually points to the problem’s root cause.

quiz.q: Why would Varma not ban coaching classes, judging by his analogy of a daily fever of 103?
quiz.a: You don’t ban paracetamol for a fever; you find what is causing it.

quiz.q: In the Pai-Shah plan, how many qualify in stage one, and how are IIT seats allotted?
quiz.a: The top one lakh qualify, then the 20,000 IIT seats are drawn by lottery.

quiz.q: Which old exam gave a third of its weight to an interview, as Ajay Shah remembers it?
quiz.a: The National Talent Search, whose panel asked him what he did in his spare time.

quiz.q: What has India normalised, according to Varma, even as everyone can buy a shampoo?
quiz.a: That good quality education is a scarce resource, rationed through entrance exams.
